summary: Defines the ALTO Transport Information Publication Service (TIPS). The original ALTO protocol is based on simple sequential HTTP/1.1 request and reply, and RFC 8895 incremental updates use Server-Sent Events. TIPS provides another way to publish ALTO information and its updates to clients.

eli5.summary: Instead of asking for the newest news again and again, you subscribe and get changes as they happen. TIPS does this for network information used to pick good connections.

questions: how does tips differ from alto sse
subtitle: How an ALTO server hands out network-information updates one numbered step at a time, over plain HTTP that clients can fetch in parallel.

tldr.problem: The ALTO base protocol only sends whole resources, and the earlier incremental scheme (ALTO/SSE) funnels updates through one ordered event stream that cannot use the parallel streams of HTTP/2 and HTTP/3.
tldr.mechanism: The server builds an updates graph for a resource, where each version has a sequence number and each edge is a snapshot or an incremental update. Clients fetch edges with ordinary GET requests at predictable URLs, and can long poll for the next one.
tldr.outcome: Clients choose when and how to pull updates, concurrently and out of order, over HTTP/1.1, HTTP/2 or HTTP/3. TIPS is meant to complement ALTO/SSE, not replace it.

facts.label: Incremental formats
facts.value: JSON merge patch or JSON patch

today: RFC 9569 is a Proposed Standard published in September 2024, and the unit metadata lists no RFC that obsoletes or updates it. It sits alongside RFC 8895 (ALTO/SSE) as a second way to deliver ALTO updates.

sections.title: Why ALTO Needs a New Transport
sections.content:
The Application-Layer Traffic Optimization (ALTO) protocol lets network applications get network status information. Before this RFC there were two ways to move that information. The base protocol (RFC 7285) sends the complete content of a resource each time. ALTO/SSE (RFC 8895) lets a client ask for updates to a set of resources, and the server pushes them over Server-Sent Events.

Both were designed for HTTP/1.1. They still work over HTTP/2 and HTTP/3, but cannot use their features well. The base protocol has no incremental updates at all, so a small change means resending the whole resource. ALTO/SSE adds its own multiplexing on top of HTTP, assumes a single ordered channel from server to client, and gives individual updates no identifier. Without an identifier, updates cannot be sent on separate HTTP/2 or HTTP/3 streams. It is also push-only, so the client cannot decide how and when to receive updates.

The Transport Information Publication Service (TIPS) fixes this with an incremental RESTful design. The RFC is clear about the trade-off: TIPS optimizes throughput through concurrent, out-of-order transfer, while ALTO/SSE optimizes latency because new events go out immediately. TIPS has no built-in session management or server push, so the RFC sees it as a complement to ALTO/SSE.
sections.eli5: The old ways either sent you the whole big book every time, or read you changes one by one in a fixed order. TIPS lets you ask for exactly the page you want, whenever you want.

sections.title: The Updates Graph
sections.content:
For each monitored resource, the server keeps a TIPS view. Its main part is the updates graph: a directed acyclic graph where each node is a version of the resource, named by a sequence number, and each edge is an update item. An update item is either a snapshot (a full replacement) or an incremental update (a JSON merge patch or JSON patch). Version 0 is reserved for the initial empty state. A tag, in the same format as the ALTO version tag, identifies the content of a node.

An update between consecutive versions (i to i+1) is mandatory. An update that skips versions is an optional shortcut. Versions are path independent: any route to the same node gives the same content. If a client holds version 103 and the latest is 105, it can fetch 105 as a snapshot, apply 103 to 104 and 104 to 105, or take a shortcut from 103 to 105 if one exists.

A server may compact or extend the graph, but it MUST keep three invariants. Continuity: every version between the smallest non-zero version (start-seq) and the latest (end-seq) exists. Feasibility: the server MUST provide a snapshot of start-seq. Right shift only: over time the start and end of the range can only move up, never down. These let clients reach any available state and guess the URL of the next update.
sections.eli5: Think of a photo album where each page has a number. You can jump straight to a full copy of a page, or flip forward one page at a time, and the album never loses the pages you need to catch up.

sections.title: Workflow and Update URLs
sections.content:
A client first asks the TIPS frontend (TIPS-F) to open a view for the resource it wants to monitor. The server answers with a URI to the root of a TIPS view (TIPS-V) and a summary: the start-seq, the end-seq and a recommended first edge to fetch. The client then pulls edges one after another.

URLs follow a fixed template, <tips-view-uri>/ug/<i>/<j>, for the update item from version i to version j. Because sequence numbers grow by exactly one, a client can build the URL of an update that does not exist yet, <end-seq>/<end-seq + 1>, and the server holds the request until the update is ready. That technique is long polling. Update items are read-only, so they are fetched with HTTP GET.

A server MAY close a TIPS view at any time, for example under high load or client inactivity. A request for a closed view gets 404 (Not Found) and the client must ask for a new view. If resources allow, the server SHOULD avoid closing views that have active polling requests or have recently served responses.
sections.eli5: You get a library card number and a rule for naming books by number. Because the numbers go up by one, you can ask for the next book before it is written, and the librarian tells you as soon as it arrives.

sections.title: Announcing and Opening a TIPS View
sections.content:
A server announces a TIPS resource in its Information Resource Directory (IRD) with media type application/alto-tips+json. Its capabilities list incremental-change-media-types, which MUST be application/merge-patch+json, application/json-patch+json or both. Where a merge patch cannot express the change faithfully (a null value would delete a field, which may not be what is meant), the server MUST choose JSON patch. The uses list names the resources the TIPS resource can serve, and the RFC RECOMMENDS a set closed under dependency, so that a cost map is offered together with the network map it depends on.

To open a view, the client sends an HTTP POST with media type application/alto-tipsparams+json and a body with resource-id, plus an optional tag (the version it already has) and an optional input for POST-mode resources. The response is application/alto-tips+json with tips-view-uri and tips-view-summary. A server MUST NOT reuse a view URI for different views. Without a tag the server MUST recommend the latest snapshot edge; with a tag it recommends either the first incremental edge from the client's version or the latest snapshot, depending on implementation, for example by comparing sizes.

Request errors return 400 (Bad Request) with an ALTO error body such as E_MISSING_FIELD or E_INVALID_FIELD_VALUE. Servers are RECOMMENDED to return 429 (Too Many Requests) when too many views are being opened. The RFC also recommends that servers offer ALTO/SSE for the TIPS resource, so clients can be told when views change.
sections.eli5: You fill in a short form saying which list you want to follow. The office hands back a slip with the address of your own copy and a note saying which page to read first.

sections.title: Pulling Updates and Next-Edge Recommendations
sections.content:
To fetch an update item the client sends GET /<tips-view-path>/ug/<i>/<j> with an Accept header matching the item's media type. For a future update it MUST list every media type that might appear. The server logic is: if the edge exists, return it; otherwise, if long polling is acceptable, queue the request until the content is ready or the request is interrupted; otherwise, return an error. Servers are RECOMMENDED to allow long polling of at least end-seq to end-seq + 1.

If a client has been away and the server has compacted the graph, the next URL may no longer exist. The client can then POST to <tips-view-path>/ug with the same body shape (without input) to get a new recommended edge. The server finds the version matching the client's tag, compares the path from that version and the path from 0 to end-seq by a cost it chooses (message count or total data size, for example), and returns the first edge of the cheaper path as a JSON merge patch.
sections.eli5: If you were away so long that the next page you wanted was thrown out, you can ask the librarian, who works out the quickest way for you to catch up.

sections.title: Operational Considerations
sections.content:
Because a client may pull the same view over several connections at once, load balancing needs care. If backend servers keep view state locally and the balancer works at Layer 4 (by TCP 5-tuple), a request can reach a server that does not hold the view. The RFC offers two fixes: store view state in a shared database so any backend can answer, or configure Layer 7 balancers to route by the tips-view-path in the URI.

Dependent resources need scheduling. A cost map version may depend on a particular network map version, so applying updates in the wrong order leaves the client with no consistent view or forces it to buffer. A client with enough buffer can long poll everything and apply updates in a consistent order, and otherwise it is RECOMMENDED to request a full snapshot.

Servers choose how to share views (one per client, or one per common resource, removed when no clients remain or never removed). They MAY also offer shortcut updates, which can speed up synchronization for clients with limited bandwidth or computation. Shortcuts cost storage, can grow the graph to the square of the number of updates in the worst case, and can reduce concurrency when the original updates touch different parts of the resource.
sections.eli5: If many helpers share one job, they must all know who has your folder. Either keep the folder in one shared cabinet, or always send you to the same helper.

sections.title: Security and Overload
sections.content:
The security considerations of the ALTO base protocol (RFC 7285) fully apply, and operators MUST follow RFC 9325 for TLS. The new update read and push services widen the attack surface in two ways the RFC names.

First, denial of service: malicious clients might open an excessive number of TIPS views to exhaust the server or block normal users. The server MAY limit active views and pending requests and answer with 429 (Too Many Requests). The RFC also mentions eviction policies, IP reputation, rate limiting and splitting the threshold across subsets of clients.

Second, client overload: the design has no flow control to slow the update rate, although TCP, HTTP/2 and QUIC offer their own limits. An overloaded client MAY drop resources that update often, and should take care because it may no longer be able to tell fresh data from stale.
sections.eli5: A bad actor could ask for so many copies that the office runs out of paper, and a slow reader could get buried by a flood of pages, so both sides need a way to say stop.
